# TOEPLITZ INFINITE GMRES FOR PARAMETERIZED LINEAR SYSTEMS

**Abstract.** We develop Toeplitz infinite GMRES for solving large sparse analytic parameterized systems _A(s)x(s_)=_z_ at many parameter values. Our method exploits a block upper triangular Toeplitz structure in the companion Krylov sequence to construct the Arnoldi process and recover solution approximations without storing full Arnoldi vectors. We derive incremental recurrences requiring O(_np_<sup>2</sup>+_p_<sup>3</sup>) arithmetic and O(_np+p_<sup>2</sup>) storage for _p_ Arnoldi steps, excluding factorization setup and assuming linear-cost coefficient actions and triangular solves. A dynamic generator-refreshing strategy addresses cancellation in this basic recurrence. Moreover, we show that the Arnoldi basis can be simply represented using one block row and a nilpotent matrix. For _A(s_) admitting a split form, we further use this structure to develop an implicitly rebased method. A residual lower bound for square-summable Taylor coefficients explains the effect of scaling outside the unit disk. Theoretical analysis and numerical experiments illustrate the computational efficiency of the proposed methods.

**Key words.** parameterized linear systems, Krylov methods, infinite Arnoldi, Toeplitz matrices, companion linearization

**MSC codes.** 65F10, 65F15, 65F50, 65H17

### 1. Introduction.

We consider the repeated solution of

\(A(s)x(s)=z,s\in\mathbb{C},\)

where \(A(s)\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}\) is large, sparse, and analytic, and \(z\in\mathbb{C}^n\) is fixed. Such systems arise in parameter-dependent partial differential equations, transfer-function evaluation, and contour-integral methods for nonlinear eigenvalue problems. When many parameter values are required, factoring each matrix _A(s_) separately is often too expensive.

GMRES [19] methods for shifted linear systems exploit Krylov shift invariance to reuse a common search space [7]. Infinite GMRES (infGMRES) [10] applies this principle to analytic parameterized systems through a Taylor companion linearization. It constructs one Arnoldi factorization for all parameter values and solves only a small parameter-dependent least-squares problem for each _s_. Extensions include inexact preconditioning [6] and a two-level orthogonal Arnoldi (TOAR) implementation for contour-integral nonlinear eigensolvers [16]. Related compact representations appear in infinite and tensor infinite Arnoldi methods [11-13,18,20] and in TOAR methods [17,22] for polynomial linearizations [15], as well as in the compact rational Krylov (CORK) framework [21].

Constructing this Arnoldi basis is still expensive. Suppose that coefficient-matrix products and triangular solves using one stored LU factorization require O(_n_) arithmetic. For _p_ steps, direct infGMRES then has O(_np_<sup>3</sup>) arithmetic and O(_np_<sup>2</sup>) storage complexity. With TOAR techniques, TOAR infGMRES reduces storage complexity to O(_np+p_<sup>3</sup>), but still needs O(_np_<sup>3</sup>+_p_<sup>4</sup>) arithmetic complexity due to the construction of full Arnoldi vectors.

Our approach exploits the Toeplitz structure in the companion Krylov sequence and updates only the QR data needed for solution recovery. Fast QR methods for

<tbc>scalar and block Toeplitz matrices \[4,5\] motivate our approach. We first derive an incremental recurrence for the needed QR data, with only O(_np_<sup>2</sup>+_p_<sup>3</sup>) arithmetic and O(_np+p_<sup>2</sup>) storage complexity. However, this approach will suffer from numerical cancellation. So we address this cancellation through dynamic generator-refreshing, even though it will add extra computational cost. The dynamic method further motivates us to use the first block row of the orthogonal basis of the Toeplitz matrix as the basis to construct the Arnoldi vectors. Based on this idea, we give a structured representation of the Arnoldi basis. Under an additional split form assumption of _A(s_), we use this structured representation to give the implicitly rebased method, which is both fast and stable in numerical experiments.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews infGMRES. Section 3 uses the block Toeplitz structure to derive the incremental and dynamic algorithms. Section 4 further explores the structure of the Arnoldi basis and develops the implicitly rebased method. Section 5 establishes the residual lower bound of infGMRES and explains the effect of scaling. Section 6 applies our algorithms to several numerical experiments to illustrate their performance. Conclusions are given in Section 7.

**2. Review of infGMRES.** We first introduce the infGMRES framework \[6\]. Throughout, assume that \(z\neq 0\), _A_<sub>0</sub>:=_A_(0) is nonsingular, and _A(s_) is analytic near the origin. Its Taylor expansion is<tbc>

\(A(s)=\sum_{j=0}^\infty A_js^j,A_j:=\frac{A^{(j)}(0)}{j!},\) (2.1)

<tbc>and its degree-_q_ truncation is \(A_q(s)=\sum_{j=0}^qA_js^j\). For any _s_ such that _A<sub>q</sub>(s_) is nonsingular, the solution _x<sub>q</sub>(s_) of _A<sub>q</sub>(s)x<sub>q</sub>(s_)=_z_ is equivalent to the first _n_ elements of the solution of<tbc>

\((\mathcal{L}_0-s\mathcal{L}_1)v(s)=\text{vec}_0(z),\text{vec}_0(z):=\left[z^T0\cdots 0\right]^T\in\mathbb{C}^{(q+1)n},\)

<tbc>with<tbc>

<tbc>Then \(\widetilde{x}(s)=[I_n,0,\dots,0]\mathcal{L}_0^{-1}\mathcal{U}_my_s\) approximates _x<sub>q</sub>(s_).

The name _infinite GMRES_ comes from extending this construction to an infinite- dimensional companion linearization \[10\]. The starting vector \(\mathrm{vec}_0(z)/\|z\|_2\) has only its first block nonzero. Multiplication by \(\mathcal{L}_1\mathcal{L}_0^{-1}\) increases the number of potentially nonzero blocks by at most one, and Arnoldi orthogonalization preserves the remaining zero blocks. Thus, in exact arithmetic, the first _p_ Arnoldi steps are identical for every _q_ greater than or equal to _p_, up to appending zero blocks to the basis vectors. The reduced least-squares problems and the recovered approximations \(\widetilde{x}(s)\) are consequently independent of _q_ as well. We may therefore formally let \(q\rightarrow\infty\) and interpret these iterates as GMRES applied to the infinite companion linearization of the full Taylor series. Each iteration still requires only finitely many active blocks and Taylor coefficients, so the infinite matrix is never formed. Omitting the zero tails introduces no truncation error into these iterates.

## 3. Toeplitz infinite GMRES.

### 3.1. Block Toeplitz motivation.

The preconditioned companion matrix is

\(\mathcal{L}_1\mathcal{L}_0^{-1}=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c c c }
0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
A_0^{-1} & -A_0^{-1}A_1 & -A_0^{-1}A_2 & \cdots & -A_0^{-1}A_q \\
I & 0 &  &  &  \\
 &  & \ddots & \ddots &  \\
 &  &  & I & 0
\end{array}\right].\)

Now we consider the structure of \(\mathcal{K}_m(\mathcal{L}_1\mathcal{L}_0^{-1},\mathrm{vec}_0(z))\). Define

(3.1) \(a_1:=A_0^{-1}z,a_m:=-A_0^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}A_ja_{m-j},\forall m\ge 2.\)

Direct multiplication gives

\(\mathcal{K}_m(\mathcal{L}_1\mathcal{L}_0^{-1},\mathrm{vec}_0(z))=\mathrm{Range}\left[\begin{array}{ c c }
z & 0 \\
0 & V_{m-1} \\
0 & 0
\end{array}\right],\)

where

\(V_m:=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c c c }
a_1 & a_2 & a_3 & \cdots & a_m \\
a_1 & a_2 & \cdots & a_{m-1} \\
 & \ddots & \ddots & \vdots \\
 &  & a_1 & a_2 \\
 &  &  & a_1
\end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{C}^{mn\times m},\forall m.\)

Because \(a_1\neq 0\), so _V<sub>m</sub>_ has full column rank. We use its unique thin QR factorization _V<sub>m</sub>=Q<sub>m</sub>R<sub>m</sub>_, with a positive real diagonal in _R<sub>m</sub>_. These factorizations are nested because the first _m_-1 columns of _V<sub>m</sub>_ equal \([V_{m-1}^T,0]^T\).

This structure already reduces infGMRES to QR factorization of Toeplitz matrix _V<sub>m</sub>_. Using the coordinates under _V<sub>m</sub>_, we can prove that the reduced least-squares problem and approximate solution in infGMRES are

(3.2) \(\mathrm{min}_{y\in\mathbb{C}^m}\left\|\left[\begin{array}{ c c c }
\|z\|_2 & 0 \\
0 & R_m
\end{array}\right]\left(\left[\begin{array}{ c }
I_m \\
0_{1\times m}
\end{array}\right]-s\left[\begin{array}{ c }
0_{1\times m} \\
I_m
\end{array}\right]\right)y-\|z\|_2e_1\right\|_2,\widetilde{x}(s)=[a_1,\dots,a_m]y.\)

To see this, we represent a vector in \(\mathcal{K}_m(\mathcal{L}_1\mathcal{L}_0^{-1},\mathrm{vec}_0(z))\) by \(v_m(y)=\left[\begin{array}{ c c } z & 0 \\ 0 & V_{m-1} \\ 0 & 0 \end{array}\right]y.\) Its lifted residual satisfies \((I-s\mathcal{L}_1\mathcal{L}_0^{-1})v_m(y)-\mathrm{vec}_0(z)\)
\(=\left[\begin{array}{ c c } z & 0 \\ 0 & V_m \\ 0 & 0 \end{array}\right]\left(\left[\begin{array}{ c } I_m \\ 0_{1\times m} \end{array}\right]-s\left[\begin{array}{ c } 0_{1\times m} \\ I_m \end{array}\right]\right)y-\mathrm{vec}_0(z)\)
\(=\left[\begin{array}{ c c } z/\|z\|_2 & 0 \\ 0 & Q_m \\ 0 & 0 \end{array}\right]\left(\left[\begin{array}{ c c } \|z\|_2 & 0 \\ 0 & R_m \end{array}\right]\left(\left[\begin{array}{ c } I_m \\ 0_{1\times m} \end{array}\right]-s\left[\begin{array}{ c } 0_{1\times m} \\ I_m \end{array}\right]\right)y-\|z\|_2e_1\right).\) The columns of diag(_z/_\(\|z\|_2,Q_m\)) are orthonormal, so this factorization preserves the residual norm and leads to the minimization in (3.2). Moreover, the first block row of \(\mathcal{L}_0^{-1}v_m(y)\) is \[_a_1_,...,am_\]_y_, which gives the approximate solution. A direct QR of _Vm_ can be implemented in O(_nm_2+_m_3) arithmetic operations by modifying the previous Toeplitz QR methods \[4,5\]. However, these methods are undesirable when \(\{a_k\}_{k=1}^m\) becomes nearly aligned or increases exponentially, which can be caused by the recursive formula (3.1). In these cases, the QR factorization of _Vm_ will lose accuracy. Meanwhile, the ill-conditioned _Rm_ will also make minimizing (3.2) unreliable. We therefore turn to the original Arnoldi process of infGMRES and develop an incremental recurrence that updates only the QR data needed for solution recovery. The following lemma shows the needed QR data. Lemma 3.1 (Arnoldi process from Toeplitz QR). _For_ \(m\ge 2\)_, let Vm=QmRm be a thin QR factorization, then the Hessenberg matrix in_ (2.3) _is_ (3.3) \(\underline{H_m}=\left[\begin{array}{ c c } 0 & 0_{1\times(m-1)} \\ \frac{\|a_1\|_2}{\|z\|_2}e_1 & R_m(1:m,2:m)R_{m-1}^{-1} \end{array}\right].\) _Moreover, if ys minimizes_ (2.4)_, then the approximate solution is_ (3.4) \(\widetilde{x}(s)=\left[\frac{a_1}{\|z\|_2},[a_2,\dots,a_m]R_{m-1}^{-1}\right]y_s.\) _Proof._ The Krylov structure and the nested QR factorizations give \(\mathcal{U}_m=\left[\begin{array}{ c c } z & 0 \\ \|z\|_2 & 0 \\ 0 & Q_{m-1} \\ 0 & 0 \end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{ c c } z & 0 \\ 0 & V_{m-1} \\ 0 & 0 \end{array}\right]\left[\frac{1}{\|z\|_2} & 0 \\ 0 & R_{m-1}^{-1} \end{array}\right]\) By direct multiplication, we obtain \(\mathcal{L}_1\mathcal{L}_0^{-1}\mathcal{U}_m=\left[\begin{array}{ c } 0_{n\times m} \\ V_m \end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{ c } 1 \\ \|z\|_2 \\ R_{m-1}^{-1} \end{array}\right]\)

We compute the thin QR factorization (3.7) \(\left[\begin{array}{ c } P_1[u_2,\dots,u_m] \\ I_{m-1} \end{array}\right]=\widehat{Q}_{m-1}\widehat{R}_{m-1},\) which can be updated by incremental Gram-Schmidt, at a cost of O(_nm+m_2) arithmetic operations at step _m_. Then the middle factor in (3.6) satisfies \(\left[\begin{array}{ c c } a_1 & [u_2,\dots,u_m] \\ 0 & I_{m-1} \end{array}\right]=[g_1,\widehat{Q}_{m-1}]\left[\begin{array}{ c c } \|a_1\| & a_1^*[u_2,\dots,u_m]/\|a_1\|_2 \\ 0 & \widehat{R}_{m-1} \end{array}\right].\) Substituting this QR factorization into (3.6) yields (3.8) \(Q_m=\left[\begin{array}{ c c } I_n & 0 \\ 0 & Q_{m-1} \end{array}\right][g_1,\widehat{Q}_{m-1}],\) (3.9) \(R_m=\left[\begin{array}{ c c } \|a_1\| & \left(a_1^*[u_2,\dots,u_m]/\|a_1\|\right)R_{m-1} \\ 0 & \widehat{R}_{m-1}R_{m-1} \end{array}\right].\) From the first _n_ rows of (3.8), we obtain (3.10) \(q_{1,1}=a_1/\|a_1\|,[q_{1,2},\dots,q_{1,m}]=\widehat{Q}_{m-1}(1:n,:).\) On the other hand, applying (3.9) and \(S_m=R_m(:,2:m)R_{m-1}^{-1}\) gives (3.11) \(S_m=\left[\begin{array}{ c } a_1^*[u_2,\dots,u_m]/\|a_1\| \\ \widehat{R}_{m-1} \end{array}\right].\) Thus, we have obtained _q_1_,m_ and _Sm_ within O(_nm+m_2) arithmetic operations at step _m_. _Updating the recovery vector u__m_+1. Notice that \(\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c } a_2 & \cdots & a_{m+1} \\ a_1 & \cdots & a_m \end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c } u_2 & \cdots & u_{m+1} \\ q_{1,1} & \cdots & q_{1,m} \end{array}\right]R_m.\) Let \(t_m=R_me_m\in\mathbb{C}^m\), then \(a_{m+1}=[u_2,\dots,u_{m+1}]t_m,\)
\(a_m=[q_{1,1},\dots,q_{1,m}]t_m.\) If we can compute _tm_, then we can compute _u__m_+1 from \[_u_2_,...,u__m_+1\]_tm=a__m_+1, with O(_nm_) arithmetic cost. By \(S_mt_{m-1}=R_m(:,2:m)R_{m-1}^{-1}R_{m-1}e_{m-1}=R_m(:,2:m)e_{m-1}=t_m,\) we can get the recurrence for _tm_: \(t_1=\|a_1\|,t_m=S_mt_{m-1},m\ge 2.\) Thus, we have derived incremental recurrences for _q_1_,m_, _Sm_, and _um_ that require only O(_nm+m_2) arithmetic operations at step _m_. The resulting algorithm is summarized in Algorithm 3.1. Let _F_LU(_n_) denote the cost of factoring _A_0 and _S_LU(_n_) the cost of one pair of triangular solves with the stored factors. If nnz(_Aj_)=O(_n_), the construction

\(F_\mathrm{LU}(n)+pS_\mathrm{LU}(n)+\mathcal{O}(np^2+p^3).\)

Storing \(\{a_m\}_{m=1}^p\), \(\{u_m\}_{m=2}^p\), \(\widehat{Q}_{p-1}\), \(\widehat{R}_{p-1}\) and _S<sub>p</sub>_ requires O(_np+p_<sup>2</sup>). In the complexity bounds below, we omit the common arithmetic cost _F_<sub>LU</sub>(_n_)+_pS_<sub>LU</sub>(_n_) and the storage of LU-factors.

**3.3. Cancellation in the recovery recurrence.** Algorithm 3.1 can lose stability. The main unstable step is computing _u<sub>m</sub>_:<tbc>

(3.12) \(u_m=\frac{a_m-[u_2,\dots,u_{m-1}]t_{m-1}(1:m-2)}{t_{m-1}(m-1)}.\)

<tbc>Let<tbc>

\(c_m=[u_2,\dots,u_{m-1}]t_{m-1}(1:m-2).\)

<tbc>This step subtracts _c<sub>m</sub>_ from _a<sub>m</sub>_ and divides by _t_<sub>_m_-1</sub>(_m_-1). A standard cancellation indicator is

\(\kappa_m^\mathrm{canc}=\frac{\|a_m\|_2+\|c_m\|_2}{\|a_m-c_m\|_2}.\)

When \(\{a_m\}_{m=1}^p\) becomes nearly linearly dependent, \(\kappa_m^\mathrm{canc}\) can be large and measures the potential amplification caused by the subtraction. The unmodified Toeplitz method then propagates the resulting error.

<tbc>Assume that we have just finished step _m_ of Toeplitz infGMRES. Now we wish to determine whether using equation (3.12) to update _u_<sub>_m_+1</sub> at step _m_+1 will cause severe cancellation. This means that we need an indicator to estimate \(\kappa_{m+1}^\text{canc}\), with the known quantities at step _m_.

To estimate this cancellation, we use the computable indicator

(3.13) \(\eta_m=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
\frac{2\|G_mS_mt_m(1:m-1)\|_2}{|t_m(m)|\|u_m\|_2}, & |t_m(m)|\|u_m\|_2>0, \\
+\infty, & |t_m(m)|\|u_m\|_2=0,
\end{array}\right.\)

where _G<sub>m</sub>_:=\[_q_<sub>1,1</sub>_,...,q_<sub>1_,m_</sub>\] is the first block row of _Q<sub>m</sub>_.

By the definitions of _G<sub>m</sub>_ and _S<sub>m</sub>_, we have

\(G_mS_m=[q_{1,1},\dots,q_{1,m}]R_m(:,2:m)R_{m-1}^{-1}=[a_2,\dots,a_m]R_{m-1}^{-1}=[u_2,\dots,u_m].\)

Thus, with _c_<sub>_m_+1</sub>=\[_u_<sub>2</sub>_,...,u<sub>m</sub>_\]_t<sub>m</sub>_(1:_m_-1), the numerator of \(\eta_m\) is 2\(\|c_{m+1}\|_2\). So

\(\frac{\eta_m}{\kappa_{m+1}^\text{canc}}=\frac{2\|c_{m+1}\|_2}{\|a_{m+1}\|_2+\|c_{m+1}\|_2}\frac{\|u_{m+1}\|_2}{\|u_m\|_2}.\)

By the reverse triangle inequality, the first ratio on the right differs from one by at most \(1/\kappa_{m+1}^\text{canc}\). Hence when \(\kappa_{m+1}^\text{canc}\) is large, \(\eta_m\) tracks prospective cancellation up to \(\|u_{m+1}\|_2/\|u_m\|_2\) and is of the same order when the norms of consecutive recovery vectors are comparable.

**3.4. Dynamic stabilization.** To weaken the cancellation, we recover selected Arnoldi vectors when the cancellation is detected. Here we consider how to construct selected Arnoldi vectors.

Because of the Toeplitz structure of _V<sub>m</sub>_, there exist vectors \(e^{i,m}\in\mathbb{C}^m\) satisfying

(3.14) \(q_{i,m}=G_me^{i,m},1\le i\le m.\)

Here we can always assume _e<sup>i,m</sup>_ is padded with zeros to arbitrarily large length.

Lemma 3.2 (Block recovery). _The recurrence of_ {_e<sup>i,m</sup>_} _is_

(3.15) \(e^{1,m}=e_m,\)

(3.16) \(e^{i,m}=\frac{e^{i-1,m-1}-\sum_{k=i}^{m-1}S_m(k,m-1)e^{i,k}}{S_m(m,m-1)},2\le i\le m.\)

_Proof._ The relation _e_<sup>1_,m_</sup>=_e<sub>m</sub>_ follows directly from the identity _q_<sub>1_,m_</sub>=_G<sub>m</sub>e<sub>m</sub>_. Moreover,

(3.17) \(Q_mS_m=Q_mR_m(:,2:m)R_{m-1}^{-1}=\left[\begin{array}{ c }
[u_2,\dots,u_m] \\
Q_{m-1}
\end{array}\right].\)

For \(2\le i\le m\), taking block row _i_ and column _m_-1 of (3.17) and using _q<sub>i,k</sub>_=0 for _k\<i_ gives

\(q_{i-1,m-1}=\sum_{k=i}^mS_m(k,m-1)q_{i,k}.\)

Solving for _q<sub>i,m</sub>_, using _G<sub>k</sub>=G<sub>m</sub>_(:,1:_k_), and zero-padding yields the recurrence. \(\square\)

At a refresh step _m_, we reconstruct _q_1_,m__,...,qm,m_ from (3.14) and replace the generator sequence \(\{a_k\}_{k=1}^m\) by \(a_i^\mathrm{new}=q_{m-i+1,m},i=1,\dots,m.\) Then we continue the Arnoldi process using \(\{a_i^\mathrm{new}\}\) and \(t_m^\mathrm{new}=e_m\). Suppose that at some step \(k\ge m\), we have \(\left[\begin{array}{ c } a_k^\mathrm{new} \\ \vdots \\ a_1^\mathrm{new} \end{array}\right]=Q_kt_k^\mathrm{new},\) while by definition this equation holds at the case _k=m_. By the recurrence formula of \(\{a_i^\mathrm{new}\}\) and (3.5), \(a_{k+1}^\mathrm{new}=-A_0^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^kA_ia_{k+1-i}^\mathrm{new}\)
\(=-A_0^{-1}[A_1,\dots,A_k]Q_kt_k^\mathrm{new}=[u_2,\dots,u_{k+1}]t_k^\mathrm{new}.\) Combining this with (3.17) gives \(\left[\begin{array}{ c } a_{k+1}^\mathrm{new} \\ a_k^\mathrm{new} \\ \vdots \\ a_1^\mathrm{new} \end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{ c } [u_2,\dots,u_{k+1}] \\ Q_k \end{array}\right]t_k^\mathrm{new}=Q_{k+1}S_{k+1}t_k^\mathrm{new}.\) Thus, \(t_{k+1}^\mathrm{new}=S_{k+1}t_k^\mathrm{new}\) preserves the relationship between the generators and their coordinates, allowing the basic recurrence to continue unchanged. With these techniques and the cancellation indicator \(\eta_m\) defined in (3.13), we propose Dynamic Toeplitz infGMRES (Dynamic TiGMRES); see Algorithm 3.2. Refreshing at _m=m_1_,...,mr_ Arnoldi steps needs about \(2n\sum_{j=1}^rm_j^2\) extra operations, because of the effort required for computing the vectors \(\{q_{i,m_k}\},1\le i\le m_k,1\le k\le r\). Algorithm 3.2 refreshes during the first half of the iterations and when \(\eta_m\ge\tau\) thereafter, using the indicator and QR update above. The reason for refreshing every step during the first half is that precision of the early steps will deeply affect the latter steps. And the cost is \(2n\sum_{j=2}^{\lfloor p/2\rfloor} j^2\approx\frac{1}{12}np^3\), which is only about \(\frac{1}{8}\) of the time that refreshing all steps takes. In practice, a suitably chosen threshold \(\tau\) can balance stability and efficiency, as we will see in Section 6. In the extreme case \(\tau=0\), Dynamic TiGMRES will refresh at every step, leading to its \(\frac{2}{3}np^3+\mathcal{O}(np^2+p^4)\) arithmetic and O(_np+p_3) storage complexity. We call this variant fully refreshed TiGMRES. For TOAR infGMRES, two-level orthogonalization costs O(_nm+m_3) at step _m_ \[16\]. Its _m_ dense _n_-by-_m_ basis products add 2_nm_2 flops per step. The total arithmetic cost over _p_ steps is therefore \(\frac{2}{3}np^3+\mathcal{O}(np^2+p^4)\). Thus fully refreshed TiGMRES and TOAR infGMRES have identical arithmetic and storage complexity. The main difference between the two algorithms is: At step _m_, fully refreshed TiGMRES uses _Gm_ as the basis to construct the full Arnoldi vectors, while TOAR infGMRES uses the orthonormal basis of the column space of _Gm_ to construct them. **4.3. Incremental evaluation of matrix-function actions.** The recovery formula (4.5) requires the vectors \(\phi_\ell(K_m)e_m\). We now describe how to update these vectors as _K<sub>m</sub>_ gains a column. Since \(K_m^m=0\), evaluating an analytic function at _K<sub>m</sub>_ requires only its Taylor polynomial of degree at most _m_-1. Moreover, the nested form of _K<sub>m</sub>_ implies that \(\phi_\ell(K_{m-1})\) is the leading principal block of \(\phi_\ell(K_m)\) \[9\]. The following application-specific updates attain the O(_m_<sup>2</sup>) cost per step.

_Fixed-degree polynomials._ Let _f_ have a fixed degree _r_. Horner’s rule computes \(\phi(K_m)e_m\) in O(_rm_<sup>2</sup>)=O(_m_<sup>2</sup>) operations.

_Rational functions._ Let _f=P/Q_ and assume \(Q(0)\neq 0\). Since _P-f_(0)_Q_ is divisible by _z_, \(\phi(K_m)\) can be evaluated as

\(\phi(K_m)=Q(K_m)^{-1}\left(\frac{P-f(0)Q}{z}\right)(K_m).\)

The quotient in parentheses is a polynomial. Because _K<sub>m</sub>_ is strictly upper triangular, _Q(K<sub>m</sub>_) is upper triangular with the nonzero diagonal entry _Q_(0). For fixed degrees, updating the last column and solving the triangular system cost O(_m_<sup>2</sup>).

_Affine square roots._ For \(f(z)=\gamma\sqrt{c+\omega z}\) with \(c\neq 0\), choose the analytic branch by fixing the scalar value \(\sqrt{c}\), and define \(T_m=(I+(\omega/c)K_m)^{1/2}\). If \(K_m=[\genfrac..{pt}{2}{K_{m-1}}{0}k_0]\), then<tbc>

\(T_m=\left[\begin{array}{ c c }
T_{m-1} & t \\
0 & 1
\end{array}\right],(T_{m-1}+I)t=(\omega/c)k,\)

<tbc>which is the scalar-border form of the classical triangular square-root recurrence \[3\]. The divided difference satisfies

\(\phi(K_m)e_m=\gamma\frac{\omega}{\sqrt{c}}(T_m+I)^{-1}e_m.\)

<tbc>Both _T_<sub>_m_-1</sub>+_I_ and _T<sub>m</sub>+I_ are upper triangular with diagonal entries 2. The two triangular solves therefore cost O(_m_<sup>2</sup>).

_Exponentials and trigonometric functions._ For \(f(z)=\mathrm{exp}(\alpha z)\), we specialize the incremental triangular evaluation strategy of \[14\] to the coupled exponential and divided-difference quantities. Let _r_<sub>13</sub>(_z_)=_P_<sub>13</sub>(_z)/Q_<sub>13</sub>(_z_) be the \[13/13\] Padé approximant to the exponential function _e<sup>z</sup>_, normalized by _P_<sub>13</sub>(0)=_Q_<sub>13</sub>(0)=1. Using the binary64 threshold \(\theta_{13}=5.371920351148152\) from \[8,  2.3\], we choose<tbc>

\(\nu=\lceil\mathrm{log}_2\mathrm{max}\{1,|\alpha|/\theta_{13}\}\rceil,h=\alpha/2^\nu,\)

<tbc>so that the scaling is fixed throughout the nested updates. Define<tbc>

\(D_h(z)=\frac{P_{13}(hz)-Q_{13}(hz)}{z}.\)

<tbc>The numerator has zero constant term, so _D<sub>h</sub>_ is a polynomial and no inversion of the singular matrix _K<sub>m</sub>_ is involved. Initialize<tbc>

\(E^{(0)}=Q_{13}(hK_m)^{-1}P_{13}(hK_m),\Phi^{(0)}=Q_{13}(hK_m)^{-1}D_h(K_m),\)

<tbc>where _E_<sup>(0)</sup> and \(\Phi^{(0)}\) can be seen as approximate matrix-function values at _K<sub>m</sub>_ of functions _e<sup>hz</sup>_ and (_e<sup>hz</sup>_-1)_/z_, respectively. The scalar identity _e_<sup>2_hz_</sup>-1=(_e<sup>hz</sup>_-1)(_e<sup>hz</sup>_+1), with analytic continuation of the divided differences at zero, yields the recovery recurrences

\(E^{(j+1)}=(E^{(j)})^2,\Phi^{(j+1)}=\Phi^{(j)}(E^{(j)}+I),j=0,\dots,\nu-1.\)

Then \(\Phi^{(\nu)}e_m\) approximates the required action \(\phi(K_m)e_m\). Since _K<sub>m</sub>_ extends _K_<sub>_m_-1</sub> by one column, the leading blocks of all intermediate matrices can be retained from the previous step. Updating only the new last columns in the polynomial evaluations, solves, and recovery stages costs \(\mathcal{O}((13+\nu)m^2)\) arithmetic and storage. Sine and cosine are handled by fixed linear combinations of the corresponding complex-exponential actions.

Thus, both changes weaken the residual lower bound while _t\>_1. This explains why using a large weight can significantly improve the accuracy of infGMRES, especially when the Taylor coefficients are small.

## 6. Numerical experiments.

We set _p=q_ in every experiment, so _p_ is both the Taylor degree and the Arnoldi length. All experiments were run in MATLAB R2023b using eight computational threads on an exclusively allocated Linux node with two AMD EPYC 9754 processors.

We call Dynamic TiGMRES with \(\tau=0\) fully refreshed TiGMRES and use it as a baseline because it has completely identical arithmetic and storage complexities with TOAR infGMRES, as discussed in Section 3.4. Dynamic TiGMRES uses \(\tau=100\), because we want to trigger refreshing when the indicator suggests a potential loss of approximately two decimal digits.

**7. Conclusions.** In this work, we present Toeplitz infGMRES, which avoids computing full Arnoldi vectors occurring in infGMRES. To address the numerical cancellation in this method, we develop Dynamic TiGMRES, which constructs full Arnoldi vector whenever the cancellation is detected. Numerical experiments show that Dynamic TiGMRES is efficient and accurate.

We further develop a structured representation of the Arnoldi basis in infGMRES. And we apply this structure to the case when _A(s_) has a split form with a small fixed _d_, leading to IR-TiGMRES. Numerical experiments demonstrate computational advantages of IR-TiGMRES in every problem.
